title: The Hotel Towel Cards
text:
Many hotels place cards in their bathrooms asking guests to reuse their towels to help the environment. In 2008 Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini and Vladas Griskevicius tested whether a different message would work better.

They worked with a hotel in Arizona over several months. In some rooms, the card carried the standard message urging guests to help save the environment by reusing their towels. In others, the card said that most guests at the hotel had reused their towels at least once during their stay, a fact drawn from an earlier study, and invited guests to join their fellow guests in helping to save the environment. Room attendants recorded whether guests reused at least one towel.

The social norm message did better. About 44 percent of guests who saw it reused towels, compared with about 35 percent of those who saw the environmental appeal. In a second study, the most effective message was the most specific: that most guests who had stayed in this very room had reused their towels. Guests responded more to what people in a situation like theirs were doing than to general appeals or to norms of broader groups such as citizens or men and women.
lesson: People follow what others like them actually do. If you want to encourage a behavior, show that it is already common, not that too few people do it.
people: Noah Goldstein, Robert Cialdini, Vladas Griskevicius
source: Goldstein, N. J., Cialdini, R. B., and Griskevicius, V. (2008). A room with a viewpoint: Using social norms to motivate environmental conservation in hotels. Journal of Consumer Research, 35(3), 472-482.
caveat: Later replication attempts found smaller or no effects, so the size of the effect in other hotels is uncertain.
